title: EMG biofeedback training, relaxation training, and placebo for the relief of chronic back pain.
abstract: 24 patients with chronic low back pain were randomly assigned to three treatment conditions: EMG biofeedback, relaxation training, and a placebo condition. Patients were seen for eight sessions and were evaluated before Session 1 and after Session 8. Eight analyses of covariance which were adjusted for age and pretest scores were computed on the final scores to find which variables could detect significant difference between treatments. Age was included as a covariate because the differences in age between conditions were significant. Four variables with significant and nearly significant differences were chosen for analysis. The second set of analyses identified the nature of the differences among the three conditions. These included a priori planned comparisons among conditions, and paired t tests. Relaxation-trained subjects were significantly superior to subjects in the placebo condition, in decreasing pain during the function test, increasing relaxation, and decreasing Upper Trapezius EMG. They were superior to EMG Biofeedback training in increasing reported activity. Both Relaxation and EMG trained subjects were able to reduce Upper Trapezius EMG by Session 8. Relaxation-trained subjects showed significant change on eight of the 14 possible comparisons for each treatment condition. EMG biofeedback training showed significant favorable results in only one condition; the placebo condition showed no significant results. Relaxation training gave better results in reducing EMG and pain, and in increasing relaxation and activity than either EMG biofeedback alone or a placebo condition.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial explicitly included a placebo arm and reported placebo-arm (no significant) outcomes, meeting inclusion as a study of placebo response/context versus active interventions.

classification.summary: Randomized 24 chronic low back pain patients to EMG biofeedback, relaxation training, or a placebo control across eight sessions and found relaxation superior to placebo and EMG on pain, relaxation, activity, and EMG reductions; placebo showed no significant change.
classification.key_finding: Relaxation training reduced pain and trapezius EMG and increased activity versus placebo and EMG; the placebo arm showed no significant pre-post improvements.

title: Responders, nonresponders, and placebo responders among children with attention deficit disorder. Importance of a blinded placebo evaluation.
abstract: The responses to methylphenidate of 118 children with attention deficit disorder (ADD) were studied under double-blind conditions. Three distinct types of response to medication and placebo were found, as determined by teacher ratings. One group, called "responders," improved dramatically in attention and hyperactivity ratings on active medication but showed essentially no change from baseline when on placebo. The group called "nonresponders" showed minimal change in ratings on either placebo or medication. The third group, "placebo responders," showed almost as much improvement as the responders on medication, but their ratings were not very different from medication ratings during the placebo trial. The placebo responders, 18 percent of the group, would have been considered responders in a nonplacebo-controlled study. Double-blind placebo evaluation of ADD children can and should be done by practitioners to avoid medicating children who are responding to nonspecific effects of drugs.

screening.rationale: The paper's stated aim and primary analyses identified and characterized 'placebo responders' in a double-blind methylphenidate trial, making placebo response the analytic focus.

classification.summary: Classified 118 children with ADD into responders, nonresponders, and placebo responders using double-blind methylphenidate versus placebo; found 18% were placebo responders.
classification.key_finding: Found that 18% of children showed substantial improvement on placebo comparable to active medication.

title: Time course of long-term placebo therapy effects in angina pectoris.
abstract: A cohort of thirty-five patients with angina pectoris were followed-up for six months with placebo as the only anti-anginal treatment apart from short-acting nitroglycerin. Only patients with at least five attacks per week were entered into the study. Prior to the study, their average number of attacks per week was 10.3(+/- 0.9) and their average nitroglycerin tablet consumption per week was 10.6(+/- 1.2). After admission into the study, the individual dosage of placebo could be blindly titrated during the first eight weeks. Once an adequate dosage was found, it was continued for 6 months. The primary end-point was predefined success or failure of the placebo treatment. Failure was assessed on the lack of improvement, occurrence of 'side-effects', or need for other anti-anginal treatment. In 27 patients, the placebo treatment was said to be a success (95% confidence limits of the percentage of success: 60-90%). No severe cardiac event occurred (confidence limits: 0-10%). Six patients developed 'side-effects'. The number of attacks per week decreased by 48% (P less than 0.0001) during the titration period (8 weeks) and by 77% during the whole 6 months. Exercise test improved, however, less markedly.

screening.rationale: Single-group cohort administered placebo as the sole anti-anginal treatment with pre-post measurement of attacks and nitroglycerin use, making placebo response the study focus (single_group_pre_post).

classification.summary: Followed 35 angina patients given placebo tablets (titrated blindly) for six months and found large reductions in weekly angina attacks and nitroglycerin use, with modest exercise-test improvement.
classification.key_finding: Placebo treatment reduced attacks per week by 48% during titration and 77% over six months; 27/35 patients met predefined success criteria.

title: The use of aminophylline and aspirin in small animal practice: effective therapy or dangerous placebos?
journal: Seminars in veterinary medicine and surgery (small animal)
journal_abbrev: Semin Vet Med Surg Small Anim

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and title suggests clinical discussion of drug efficacy with the metaphorical term 'placebos', so insufficient information to determine whether placebo/nocebo phenomena are an explicit focus.

classification.summary: Was a 1986 veterinary review that discussed aminophylline and aspirin use in small-animal practice and questioned whether they were effective therapies or 'dangerous placebos'.

title: Alcohol and the balanced-placebo design: the role of experimenter demands in expectancy.

screening.rationale: Title indicates a balanced-placebo design investigating alcohol expectancy and experimenter demands, but no abstract or full text was available to confirm whether placebo/nocebo phenomena were the explicit analytic focus or to extract outcomes.

classification.summary: Title indicated a balanced-placebo experiment testing alcohol expectancy and experimenter demand effects, but no abstract was available to confirm results or sample size.

title: The role of self-efficacy expectancies in the prediction of pain tolerance.
abstract: The association of self-efficacy expectancies with pain tolerance on the cold pressor test was examined during treatment conditions of setting quotas alone and in conjunction with monetary reinforcement and placebos in 64 college volunteers. It was found that quota setting was an effective means of increasing cold pressor pain tolerance. The addition of monetary reinforcement of quota achievement did not enhance performance, while the addition of a placebo decreased the effectiveness of quota setting. Self-efficacy expectancies were significantly correlated with pain tolerance times and were better predictors of tolerance than pain ratings. Self-efficacy expectancies and pain tolerance times at treatment were both found to predict 1 week follow-up performance.

screening.rationale: The study manipulated a placebo condition (placebo added to quota-setting) and reported its impact on cold-pressor pain tolerance, meeting the criterion for an experimentally isolated placebo/context manipulation.

classification.summary: Examined how self-efficacy predicted cold-pressor pain tolerance across quota-setting, quota+monetary, and quota+placebo conditions and found that adding a placebo reduced the effectiveness of quota setting.
classification.key_finding: Addition of a placebo decreased the effectiveness of quota setting on cold-pressor pain tolerance (N=64).

title: Is homoeopathy a placebo response? Controlled trial of homoeopathic potency, with pollen in hayfever as model.
abstract: The hypothesis that homoeopathic potencies are placebos was tested in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The study model chosen compared the effects of a homoeopathic preparation of mixed grass pollens with placebo in 144 patients with active hayfever. The homoeopathically treated patients showed a significant reduction in patient and doctor assessed symptom scores. The significance of this response was increased when results were corrected for pollen count and the response was associated with a halving of the need for antihistamines. An initial aggravation of symptoms was noted more often in patients receiving the potency and was followed by an improvement in that group. No evidence emerged to support the idea that placebo action fully explains the clinical responses to homoeopathic drugs.

screening.rationale: Randomized, double-blind trial explicitly tested whether homeopathic potencies are placebos (stated hypothesis), making placebo phenomena the paper's focal question despite being an active-versus-placebo RCT.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial tested homeopathic grass-pollen remedy versus placebo in 144 hayfever patients and found significant reductions in patient- and doctor-rated symptoms and reduced antihistamine use in the homeopathy group.
classification.key_finding: Homeopathic potency produced greater symptom reduction and less antihistamine use than placebo; authors concluded placebo alone did not fully explain responses.

title: Useless drugs are not placebos: lessons from flunarizine and cinnarizine.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and title suggests an opinion about labeling of drugs rather than reporting empirical placebo data, so insufficient information to judge inclusion.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title argued that ineffective drugs (flunarizine, cinnarizine) should not be considered placebos, likely a commentary.

title: Follow-up of patients who improved during placebo washout.
abstract: Depressed patients who showed significant improvement after a 10-day placebo washout trial were followed for 3 months. Twenty-five relapsed and 20 remained well. Relapsing patients more frequently had a family history of depression, more had prior psychiatric treatment, their illness course was more chronic once ill, mean age of onset was younger, and fewer had obvious precipitants. More relapser had RDC diagnoses of intermittent depressive disorder. Among those with major depressive disorder, fewer relapsers met subtype criteria for simple, situational, or recurrent. Nonaffective psychiatric disorders were present in 64% of relapsers and no placebo responders who remained well. Overall, 10-day placebo responders included patients with different clinical characteristics and subsequent course.

screening.rationale: Study explicitly followed and analyzed patients who improved during a 10-day placebo washout, making placebo response the object of study (predictors of relapse).

classification.summary: Followed depressed patients who improved during a 10-day placebo washout for 3 months and compared relapse versus sustained-well groups to identify clinical predictors of relapse.
classification.key_finding: Among 45 placebo responders followed, 25 relapsed and 20 remained well; relapse was associated with family history, prior psychiatric treatment, chronic course, earlier onset, and comorbid nonaffective disorders.

title: Alcohol and simple reaction time in a vigilance setting: a placebo control study.
abstract: The present study tested whether earlier reported effects of alcohol on simple auditory and visual reaction time in a vigilance setting should be attributed to the pharmacological properties of alcohol or to subjects' expectancies as to the acute effects of alcohol. Results indicated that an expectancy interpretation can be excluded.

screening.rationale: Study experimentally manipulated expectancy versus pharmacological alcohol effects (placebo control), explicitly testing placebo/expectancy as an explanation for reaction-time changes.

classification.summary: Tested whether alcohol effects on auditory and visual simple reaction time were due to pharmacology or expectancies and found that expectancy explanations could be excluded.
classification.key_finding: Found pharmacological alcohol effects on reaction time; expectancies (placebo) did not account for the impairments.

title: Frank's "common elements" in psychotherapy: nonspecific factors and placebos.
abstract: Implications of Jerome Frank's seminal hypotheses are further considered, specifically that all psychological treatments share common elements that account for the effective treatment of a core problem shared by all patients--demoralization. The stages of psychotherapy and the potential role of suggestion, nonspecific elements, and placebo are highlighted.

screening.rationale: The paper is a theoretical/commentary focused on placebo, suggestion, and nonspecific factors in psychotherapy, fitting 'placebo_science_other' inclusion (placebo as main subject in a conceptual review).

classification.summary: Discussed Jerome Frank's common-elements view of psychotherapy and highlighted the role of suggestion, nonspecific factors, and placebo in producing clinical improvement.

title: Double blind: double talk or are there ways to do better research.
abstract: In an attempt to counteract placebo effects, scientists studying the effectiveness of medication often use the 'double blind' trial. Unfortunately, in less than 5% of the studies reported in major medical and psychiatric journals was there a check to determine whether patients and observers were blind. Between 1972 and 1983 there was increasing reliance on active placebos which attempt to mimic the effects of the medication. It is unlikely however, that patients are not aware of significantly different physiologic changes within them resulting from the different chemicals. Whenever a physician informs a subject that they may be on placebo or active treatment medication, they will spend much time in trying to guess when they are taking which. In these situations Philip's paradox will apply. This states that the more potent a therapeutic variable the less likely its efficacy can be 'proven' in a double-blind study. One can only 'prove' that medication is no more effective than placebo. To have a truly blind procedure, the active placebo must have identical physiological effects to those of the medication being studied. We are now using the patient's and the observer's awareness of changes as useful information to obtain: a guess factor, the percentage of correct guesses whether the patient is on medication or placebo; a direction factor, whether the patient considers the change beneficial or detrimental; an attributional factor, whether the change is considered to result from medication or other intervening variables. This information is usually reliable and can be analyzed with the usual statistical procedures.

screening.rationale: Paper is a theory/methods commentary focused on placebo research methodology and blinding checks, meeting inclusion for placebo_science_other (placebo-focused methodological discussion).

classification.summary: Discussed limitations of double-blind trials, active placebos, and advocated using blinding checks (guesses, attribution, direction) as useful data for placebo research.

title: Trachea noise biofeedback device to help reduce bronchospasm in asthmatics.
abstract: Evidence suggests that conscious control of bronchial smooth muscle tone may be possible. The asthmatic wheeze is caused mainly by broncho-constriction and it is hypothesized that if wheeze were consciously reduced, some bronchodilation would occur. Described here is a biofeedback device which records asthmatic tracheal noise with a microphone, and generates both an audio and visual display of the degree of wheeze sound intensity. The subject attempts to reduce wheeze using the device. Wrong information is also generated within the device so that the placebo effect can be investigated.

screening.rationale: Paper explicitly manipulated false feedback in a biofeedback device to investigate a placebo effect on bronchospasm, making placebo phenomena an explicit experimental focus.

classification.summary: Described a tracheal-noise biofeedback device for asthmatics and reported that false feedback was generated so the placebo effect on wheeze/bronchospasm could be investigated.

title: Does short term placebo treatment of chronic schizophrenia produce long term harm?
abstract: A randomised double blind placebo controlled trial is the most reliable method of assessing putative new developments in medical treatment. In schizophrenia, however, some clinicians believe that relapse contributes to long term deterioration and therefore that patients exposed to either placebo or an inactive new treatment may be put at a disadvantage in the long run if the trial leads to an additional relapse. A seven year follow up of patients included in a randomised placebo controlled trial of fluphenazine decanoate, in which 66% of the group given placebo relapsed compared with 8% of those who received the active drug, permitted examination of any long term adverse consequences in those patients who had received placebo. Seventy six (94%) of the 81 patients in the original trial were followed up. At the end of the follow up period there were no consistent or important differences in any measure of clinical or social outcome between the patients who had received placebo and those who had received the active drug. This negative finding has implications for the debate on the risk of placebo controlled trials of maintenance treatment in chronic schizophrenia.

screening.rationale: The trial explicitly tested whether short-term randomization to placebo caused long-term harm by comparing long-term clinical and social outcomes of placebo versus active-treated patients, making placebo exposure the study focus.

classification.summary: Followed patients from a randomized placebo-controlled fluphenazine trial for seven years and found no consistent long-term clinical or social differences between those originally randomized to placebo versus active drug despite higher short-term relapse on placebo.
classification.key_finding: Short-term relapse was higher in the placebo group (66% vs 8%) but there were no consistent or important differences in long-term clinical or social outcomes at seven-year follow-up.

title: Treatment for hypertension interrupted by placebo: the response of patients with high and low general health questionnaire scores.
journal: The Journal of the Royal College of General Practitioners
abstract: A study is described in which established treatment for hypertension was interrupted by placebo as part of a change to an alternative treatment.The patients involved were divided into two groups according to their score on the general health questionnaire. All the patients showed an increase in diastolic pressure after the placebo phase of the change-over but the increase was greater for patients with a high score on the general health questionnaire than it was for patients with a low score. For the patients with a high score the diastolic pressure approximated to the level recorded when the diagnosis was first made, but for patients with a low score it was considerably lower than this initial reading.The implication of this finding for the design of ;changeover' studies is discussed.

screening.rationale: Study experimentally replaced antihypertensive treatment with placebo and analyzed the blood-pressure response, focusing on placebo-induced worsening and its moderation by GHQ score.

classification.summary: Interrupted antihypertensive treatment with placebo and found diastolic blood pressure rose during the placebo phase, with larger increases in patients with higher GHQ scores.
classification.key_finding: Diastolic pressure increased after placebo substitution, and the rise was greater in patients with high general health questionnaire scores (approaching initial diagnostic levels).

title: A comparison of responses to albuterol delivered by two aerosol devices.
abstract: Nineteen outpatients with stable obstructive pulmonary disease (mean forced expiratory volume in one second [FEV1], 1.00 + 0.10 L) were evaluated for airway response to albuterol (salbutamol) administered by metered-dose inhaler and Bosch ultrasonic nebulizer (BUSN). Albuterol administered by metered-dose inhaler but not by nebulizer caused a significant increase in FEV1 and the mean forced expiratory flow over the middle half of the forced vital capacity (FEF25-75%) (p less than 0.02). Absolute increase from baseline of FEV1 and FEF25-75% was significantly greater for metered-dose inhaler (0.21 +/- 0.05 L; 0.32 +/- 0.13 L/sec) compared to ultrasonic nebulizer (0.07 +/- 0.03 L; 0.03 +/- 0.04 L/sec) (p less than 0.02). In 11 subjects (mean FEV1, 1.08 + 0.14 L), the placebo effect of inhalation of the diluent from the metered-dose inhaler (Freon) and the ultrasonic nebulizer (isotonic saline solution) was determined. Freon produced the mean increase of 1.5 percent, whereas the ultrasonic aerosol of isotonic saline solution resulted in a mean decrease of 8 percent in FEV1. Therefore, the inferior response to albuterol administered by ultrasonic nebulizer was at least in part due to the superimposed broncho-constriction occurring with ultrasonically administered saline solution. The metered-dose inhaler was more effective than the ultrasonic nebulizer for administration of albuterol in stable obstructive pulmonary disease, and the latter device is not recommended. A specific ultrasonic nebulizer should be prescribed only if its superiority to a metered-dose inhaler can be objectively documented.

screening.rationale: The paper explicitly measured and reported placebo (diluent) inhalation responses in a subset of participants, making placebo response an analytic focus.

classification.summary: Measured bronchodilator responses to albuterol delivered by two aerosol devices and reported placebo (diluent) inhalation effects, finding a small FEV1 increase with MDI diluent and an FEV1 decrease with ultrasonic saline.
classification.key_finding: In 11 subjects, inhalation of MDI diluent (Freon) produced a mean 1.5% increase in FEV1, whereas ultrasonic saline produced a mean 8% decrease, suggesting device-related placebo/nocebo effects on airway caliber.

title: A three year follow up of patients allocated to placebo, or oral or injectable gold therapy for rheumatoid arthritis.
abstract: Ninety patients randomly allocated to receive auranofin, matching placebo, or sodium aurothiomalate have been followed up for three years. Inefficacy led to cessation of treatment in 14 patients receiving auranofin, 27 receiving placebo, and one receiving sodium aurothiomalate. Twenty seven of the patients receiving placebo were reallocated within the study and 16 continued therapy at three years. This group showed similar statistically significant improvement in clinical and laboratory parameters at one, two, and three years to those on an active drug from the outset. Patients who discontinued auranofin because of inefficacy were offered sodium aurothiomalate therapy--eight patients in this group completed three years of treatment on sodium aurothiomalate and showed significant improvement in some but not all parameters. A hand radiograph erosion score showed a deterioration in 80% of patients remaining on auranofin, 75% of those on sodium aurothiomalate, and 80% of the original placebo group who continued an active drug for three years. Although more patients discontinued auranofin over the study period because of inefficacy, no difference could be shown between the degree of improvement in the subgroup who remained on auranofin and those receiving sodium aurothiomalate. No disadvantage in outcome could be shown for patients originally assigned to placebo.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial reported and analyzed the placebo arm's longitudinal clinical and laboratory improvement (placebo response) and compared outcomes with active treatment, meeting inclusion for placebo response analysis.

classification.summary: Followed 90 RA patients randomized to auranofin, placebo, or injectable gold for three years and found the original placebo group who later received active therapy showed similar significant clinical and laboratory improvement as active groups, while radiographic erosion progressed in most patients.
classification.key_finding: Patients originally assigned to placebo who continued therapy showed comparable improvements in clinical and lab measures to active-drug groups over three years, but radiographic erosion worsened in ~75–80% across groups.

title: Placebo responses: an experimental study of psychophysiological processes in asthmatic volunteers.
journal: The British journal of clinical psychology
abstract: This study evaluated the effects of placebo medication on pulmonary responses in asthmatics, and investigated the roles of expectancy and anxiety. Twelve adult asthmatics were recruited for a laboratory experiment described as a study of the effectiveness of a new bronchodilator. Distilled nebulized water was inhaled in each session. The solution was described as water in session 1 (control), while in sessions 2 and 3 subjects were told that the nebulizer contained a chemical likely to cause chest tightness and wheezing (bronchoconstrictive suggestion). Prior to the inhalation sequence in sessions 2 and 3, subjects inhaled from an aerosol that they were told contained either a powerful new drug (placebo) or a non-active substance (neutral). Pulmonary function was measured with the forced oscillation technique and spirometry, while autonomic parameters, anxiety and expectancies were also monitored. Pulmonary function deteriorated following the inhalations accompanied by bronchoconstrictive suggestion, and this effect was abolished by pre-treatment with placebo. Neither subject expectations nor changes in anxiety were associated with the experimental manipulations. The implications of these results for theories of placebo action are considered.

screening.rationale: Within-subject experimental manipulation of placebo pre-treatment and bronchoconstrictive suggestion in asthmatics directly tested placebo/nocebo effects on pulmonary function.

classification.summary: Tested placebo and bronchoconstrictive suggestion in 12 asthmatic adults across within-subject sessions and found placebo pre-treatment abolished suggestion-induced pulmonary deterioration.
classification.key_finding: Pre-treatment with a verbally described 'powerful new drug' placebo prevented bronchoconstrictive-suggestion–induced declines in pulmonary function.

title: How blind is blind? Assessment of patient and doctor medication guesses in a placebo-controlled trial of imipramine and phenelzine.
abstract: The purpose of the double blind is to protect the internal validity of a clinical trial by preventing knowledge of treatment conditions from influencing outcome or its assessment. We studied medication guesses of 137 depressed patients and/or their doctors at the end of a 6-week randomized trial of placebo, imipramine, and phenelzine. Overall, 78% of the patients and 87% of the doctors correctly distinguished between placebo and active medication. Clinical outcome, treatment condition, and their interaction each contributed to guessing accuracy, while medication experience and side effects assessed only in week 6 did not. Accuracy was high, however, even when cases were stratified for clinical outcome, indicating that other cues were available to the patients and doctors. These may include patterns and timing of side effects and clinical response not detectable in this end-point analysis.

screening.rationale: The paper's primary analysis focused on assessment of blinding/medication guesses in a placebo-controlled RCT, making placebo-related methodology the main subject (placebo science/blinding).

classification.summary: Assessed patient and physician medication guesses in a 6-week randomized trial of placebo, imipramine, and phenelzine and found high rates of correct identification of active versus placebo.
classification.key_finding: Found that 78% of patients and 87% of doctors correctly distinguished placebo from active medication (N=137).

title: Discomfort and bite force in painful masseter muscles after intramuscular injections of local anesthetic and saline solution.
abstract: Thirty women with a history of daily pain in the masseter muscles were injected with either lidocaine or saline. The participants were told that they were being given an anesthetic injection to reduce their muscular discomfort. The dentist performing the injections did not know which fluid was used. The discomfort in the masseter muscle was assessed by using Borg's new rating scale before and 10 minutes after injection. The evaluation was followed up on day 1, day 3, and day 7. Bite force was registered between the first molars on the injection side. When scale values were compared individually within groups before and after injection, a significant decrease in discomfort was found in both groups, with the exception of day 1 for the lidocaine group and days 1 and 3 in the saline group. The total lidocaine and saline groups assessed the discomfort similarly except on day 3 when the lidocaine group showed significantly less discomfort. The intraindividual force values increased significantly after injection in the saline group. This effect was not found in the lidocaine group. Despite the minor tendencies for lidocaine to have a better effect, the placebo effect was considered to be high and important.

screening.rationale: Randomized controlled injection study that analyzed placebo (saline) responses and discussed placebo effects explicitly.

classification.summary: Found that both lidocaine and saline injections reduced reported masseter discomfort and that saline injections produced a significant increase in bite force, indicating a substantial placebo response.
classification.key_finding: Both groups showed decreased discomfort versus baseline; the saline (placebo) group showed a significant post-injection increase in bite force.

title: Does informed consent influence therapeutic outcome? A clinical trial of the hypnotic activity of placebo in patients admitted to hospital.
abstract: To examine whether written informed consent might influence the results of clinical trials the effect of placebo when given with or without informed consent to patients suffering from insomnia was studied. The study was a single blind observer blinded trial, and patients were paired according to sex, age, and hospital environment. Randomisation assigned the first patient of each pair to the control group (without informed consent) or the group to give informed consent. Of the 56 patients, 26 refused to give informed consent, and the age and sex distribution of these differed significantly (p less than 0.02) from the 30 pairs of patients ultimately enrolled into the study. In this "biased" sample, the hypnotic activity of placebo was significantly higher in the control group (p less than 0.05). It is concluded that the informed consent procedure biases the results of clinical trials and might affect their general applicability.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial manipulated informed-consent disclosure to test its effect on placebo hypnotic activity, making placebo/context the explicit object of study (placebo effect via disclosure).

classification.summary: Randomized, single-blind trial tested whether written informed consent altered the hypnotic activity of placebo in hospitalized patients with insomnia and found greater placebo hypnotic effect when consent was not obtained.
classification.key_finding: Placebo produced significantly greater hypnotic activity in the group without informed consent (p < 0.05).

title: Alcohol, frustration, and aggression: an experiment using the balanced placebo design.

screening.rationale: Balanced-placebo design explicitly manipulates alcohol expectancy versus actual intoxication to test causal effects of expectation (a placebo/expectancy mechanism) on aggression.

classification.summary: Used a balanced-placebo experiment to test how alcohol administration versus alcohol expectancy influenced aggression after frustration in adult male participants.

title: Short burst oxygen treatment for breathlessness in chronic obstructive airways disease.
abstract: Most patients with chronic obstructive lung disease prescribed oxygen at home by their family doctor use it for short periods when they feel breathless. Many patients are normoxic. Nineteen patients with advanced disease and variable hypoxaemia undertook exercise until they indicated severe breathlessness on a 100 mm visual analogue scale. Air, 67% oxygen, and air delivered from a cylinder in an identical manner to the oxygen were randomly administered during the recovery periods. Respiratory rate, heart rate and oxygen and carbon dioxide tensions, estimated by transcutaneous electrodes (tcPo2, tcPco2), were measured throughout the exercise and recovery periods. The mean recovery time for breathlessness as judged by visual analogue score was significantly shorter when oxygen was used than during placebo or air recovery (p less than 0.05). The rates of return to baseline levels of respiratory and heart rates were not significantly affected by the gas inhaled. No placebo effect was detectable. It was not possible to select good responders from the results of prior physiological tests. In seven patients the study was repeated after an interval of between one week and a year. The consistency of observed response to oxygen was poor. Although recovery judged by visual analogue scores showed some consistency within individual patients and greater overall consistency than heart rate or respiratory rate, the direction of change in recovery judged by visual analogue score after the breathing of oxygen was variable. The change during the breathing of oxygen was towards improvement in both studies in three patients and towards deterioration in both studies in one patient, and it showed no consistent direction of change in the remaining three patients. It is difficult to determine which patients will derive substantial and reproducible benefit from short burst oxygen but their numbers are probably small. The results cast doubt on the justification for the current widespread prescription of oxygen cylinders for occasional use.

screening.rationale: Within-subject randomized comparison included an inert/placebo air condition and explicitly tested for placebo effects on breathlessness VAS, allowing experimental isolation of placebo versus oxygen effects.

classification.summary: Found that inhaled oxygen shortened recovery time for breathlessness versus placebo air on VAS, with no detectable placebo effect and no change in heart or respiratory rates.

title: Value of serial peak expiratory flow measurements in assessing treatment response in chronic airflow limitation.
abstract: A double blind, randomised, placebo controlled, crossover trial of prednisolone (40 mg/day for 14 days) was carried out in 33 patients with chronic airflow limitation (mean age 62 years, mean FEV1 1.01 litres, mean FEV1/FVC ratio 44%), to assess the value of serial peak expiratory flow (PEF) measurements, taken five times daily in evaluating treatment response by comparison with other objective measurements and with measurements of symptoms. The mean serial PEF after a one week run in period was 189 1 min-1, during the second week of placebo 193 1 min-1, and during the second week on prednisolone 231 1 min-1. The difference in mean PEF values between placebo and prednisolone was significant (p less than 0.01). With regard to the response to steroids of the individual patients, 13 of the 33 had a detectable trend of improvement on visual inspection of serial PEF measurements during prednisolone treatment but only one during placebo administration. Of all the objective measurements made after the run in and after each treatment phase (12 minute walking distance, FEV1, forced vital capacity (FVC), serial PEF), the serial PEF chart provided the best discrimination between placebo and prednisolone treatment. There was no statistically significant association between steroid induced improvement in serial PEF measurements and in breathlessness, partly because of placebo improvements in symptoms in those who had no improvement in serial PEF values. This study indicates the importance of making objective measurements to identify a genuine steroid response rather than relying on symptomatic improvement alone. The best simple measurement to make is serial PEF during steroid trials. This is more sensitive in detecting a steroid response than are the 12 minute walking distance, FEV1, or FVC, and is also less likely than these measurements to show spurious placebo responses.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial that reported placebo-arm symptom changes and compared placebo vs prednisolone responses, so placebo response and placebo-related measurement issues were a substantive focus.

classification.summary: Found that serial peak expiratory flow detected steroid response better than FEV1, FVC, or 12-minute walk, and that symptoms showed placebo-related improvements, underscoring the value of objective measures in steroid trials.
classification.key_finding: Serial PEF increased significantly on prednisolone versus placebo (mean second-week PEF 231 vs 193 L/min; p<0.01), while some symptom measures improved during placebo.

title: Light treatment of seasonal affective disorder in Switzerland.
abstract: Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) has been characterised by two or more depressive episodes in autumn or winter (with remission the following spring or summer), decreased energy, increased sleep, increased appetite, weight gain and carbohydrate craving. SAD patients were identified in a Swiss-German population; 22 participated in a light-therapy protocol (1 week bright white light 2,500 lux or dim yellow light 250 lux, from 06-08 h and 18-20 h). Both observer and self-ratings indicated a significant diminution of depressive symptoms with both lights. One week after withdrawal from yellow light, depression ratings relapsed to previous values; remission lasted longer after bright white light. Global VAS self-rating scales for "mood" and "well-being" however, and the Hamilton scale for atypical SAD symptoms, differentiated clearly between bright and dim light: only bright light showed an improvement that persisted after withdrawal. These results suggest that even though a placebo effect cannot be excluded, 4 h explicit light exposure/day may not be a negligible quantity. Light treatment promises to be a useful non-pharmacological intervention in certain forms of depressive illness.

screening.rationale: Randomized comparison of bright vs dim (placebo-like) light with analyses reporting placebo-like responses and differential sustained effects, so the paper examines treatment-context/placebo-related effects.

classification.summary: Randomized trial compared bright (2,500 lux) versus dim (250 lux) light for seasonal affective disorder and found both reduced depressive ratings but bright light produced more persistent remission after withdrawal.
classification.key_finding: Both bright and dim light produced symptom improvement, but bright white light yielded longer-lasting remission compared with dim yellow light.

title: Effects of nedocromil sodium and placebo delivered by pressurised aerosol in bronchial antigen challenge.

screening.rationale: Abstract unavailable and title suggests a drug efficacy trial where placebo served as comparator, so it's unclear whether placebo/nocebo effects or responses were a study focus.

classification.summary: No abstract available; paper compared nedocromil sodium with a placebo aerosol during bronchial antigen challenge in humans (asthma context) but it is unclear whether placebo effects or responses were analyzed.

title: Forget placebos--let's go for the strong stuff.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and the title suggests an opinion piece, so it's unclear whether placebo phenomena are the paper's explicit focus.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title suggests an opinion/editorial about placebo use, but text was unavailable to confirm focus on placebo science.

title: Which depressions respond to placebo?
abstract: This descriptive study of 55 outpatients with unipolar major depression compared placebo responders (n = 21) and placebo nonresponders (n = 34) with respect to demographic, diagnostic, history of illness and symptomatic features of the current episode of depression. Placebo responders were significantly more likely to be nonendogenous and were more likely to meet criteria for another Research Diagnostic Criteria diagnosis. Additionally, placebo responders were characterized by a shorter length of illness and reported a lower level of depressive symptomatology on the Beck Depression Inventory and the Carroll Rating Scale. Clinician-rated depressive symptom severity (e.g., Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression, Covi Global Anxiety Scale, and Raskin Depression Rating Scale) and demographic variables did not differentiate placebo responders from nonresponders. These data suggest candidates for antidepressant treatment and implications for antidepressant drug trials.

screening.rationale: Study explicitly analyzed characteristics of placebo responders versus nonresponders in a depression trial, making placebo response the paper's focus (rule 2).

classification.summary: Compared 55 depressed outpatients, identifying 21 placebo responders and 34 nonresponders and reporting baseline clinical and history differences associated with placebo response.
classification.key_finding: Found that placebo responders were more likely nonendogenous, had shorter illness duration, and lower self-reported depressive symptoms at baseline.

title: Treatment expectancy among psychiatric inpatients.
abstract: Treatment expectation (TE) is an important variable in treatment outcome. This study addressed two issues: The relationship of TE to treatment outcome and an identification of background and treatment variables most related to TE. As part of a cooperative study at 18 Veterans Administration Medical Centers on 79 general psychiatric wards, psychiatric inpatients were given the Veterans Adjustment Scale (VETS), and a significant other was mailed a Personal Adjustment and Role Skills Scale (PARS) at admission and 3 months after discharge. A Treatment Expectation measure was obtained from the VETS Scale at admission. Background and treatment factors also were obtained. Selected analyses controlled for the effects of patient input characteristics allowing for better outcome measures. Analyses also were cross validated. Results show that TE is related to treatment outcome and that a coterie of background and treatment variables are related to TE. Three factors especially influence TE-age, high vigor, and less alienation.

screening.rationale: Treatment expectation was measured and tested as a predictor of treatment outcome in psychiatric inpatients, which studies expectation as a mechanism relevant to placebo/nocebo phenomena.

classification.summary: Measured treatment expectation at admission in psychiatric inpatients and found expectation predicted 3-month psychosocial adjustment, with age, vigor, and less alienation related to expectation.
classification.key_finding: Found that higher treatment expectation predicted better post-discharge adjustment; age, higher vigor, and lower alienation were key correlates of expectation.
free_keywords: personal adjustment and role skills scale

title: Treatment of the premenstrual syndrome by subcutaneous estradiol implants and cyclical oral norethisterone: placebo controlled study.
abstract: The hypothesis that the many non-specific changes normally associated with cyclical ovarian activity are the primary aetiological factors in the premenstrual syndrome was tested by suppressing ovulation with subcutaneous oestradiol implants. Sixty eight women with proved premenstrual syndrome were treated under placebo controlled conditions for up to 10 months in a longitudinal study. Active treatment was combined with cyclical oral norethisterone to produce regular withdrawal periods. Symptoms were monitored with daily menstrual distress questionnaires, visual analogue scales, and the 60 item general health questionnaire. Of the 35 women treated with placebo 33 improved, giving an initial placebo response rate of 94%. The placebo effect gradually waned, but the response to the active combination was maintained for the duration of the study. Analysis of the prospective symptom ratings showed a significant superiority of oestradiol implants over placebo after two months for all six symptom clusters in the menstrual distress questionnaire. Changes seen in the retrospective assessments were less significant but the trend was the same. Treatment with oestradiol implants and cyclical progestogen was well tolerated and appears to be both rational and effective for severe cases of the premenstrual syndrome.

screening.rationale: The trial reported and analyzed a large placebo response within the placebo arm (94% improved) and described placebo effects over time, so placebo response was an object of study rather than a mere comparator.

classification.summary: Randomized trial of estradiol implants plus cyclical norethisterone for PMS found a very large placebo-arm improvement (33/35; 94%) and maintained superiority of active treatment after two months on prospective symptom ratings.
classification.key_finding: Placebo-arm initial response rate was 94% (33 of 35), with placebo effect waning over time while active treatment retained benefit.

title: Physical dependence on nicotine in gum. A placebo substitution trial.
abstract: To test whether ex-smokers become physically dependent on nicotine in gum, we entered eight ex-smokers who were using nicotine gum into a randomized, double-blind, placebo-substitution trial. When placebo was substituted, seven of the eight subjects were observed to have withdrawal symptoms and two relapsed to smoking or nicotine gum. This result suggests that physical dependence (ie, withdrawal) may be a cause of behavioral dependence on nicotine gum (ie, use of gum beyond the recommended period) and physicians should emphasize the need for gradual reduction of nicotine gum.

screening.rationale: Randomized, double-blind placebo-substitution trial that focused on withdrawal (adverse symptoms) after replacing nicotine gum with placebo, making placebo/nocebo response the study object.

classification.summary: Randomized, double-blind placebo-substitution trial in eight ex-smokers found that substituting placebo for nicotine gum produced withdrawal symptoms in seven participants and two relapsed to smoking or gum.
classification.key_finding: Seven of eight subjects developed withdrawal symptoms after placebo substitution; two relapsed to smoking or nicotine gum.

title: Facilitation of the maximum voluntary contraction in hemiplegia by concomitant cutaneous stimulation.
abstract: The effects of rapid brushing on the maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) and tonic vibratory reflex (TVR) of various muscles requiring facilitation (quadriceps, biceps femoris and tibialis anterior) were studied in two samples of hemiplegics. Brushing was studied under experimental and placebo conditions. In the first experiment, brushing produced significant facilitation of MVC and TVR in the quadriceps, replicating the findings of Spicer and Matyas (1980) and Matyas and Spicer (1980). However, the effect of the TVR failed to predict the gain in MVC that resulted from brushing. In the second sample of hemiplegics, brushing produced significant facilitation of the MVC and TVR in the biceps femoris but not in the tibialis anterior. The results for biceps femoris confirmed the results obtained with quadriceps. The failure to replicate this effect with tibialis anterior may have resulted from problems with the application of the stimulus to the relevant dermatome. Further exploration of the effect of cutaneous stimulation relating to this muscle is required to resolve this issue. The results of this experiment, with its replication of the facilitatory effect of brushing on TVR and MVC in two muscle groups, suggest that investigations of the effect of cutaneous stimulation on the acquisition and retention of voluntary movement should now take place.

screening.rationale: Empirical human study that contrasted cutaneous stimulation with a placebo condition and reported facilitation of MVC and TVR, addressing the causal effect of stimulation (placebo-effect style controlled comparison).

classification.summary: Found that rapid brushing (versus placebo stimulation) significantly facilitated maximum voluntary contraction and tonic vibratory reflex in hemiplegic patients for quadriceps and biceps femoris but not tibialis anterior.
classification.key_finding: Brushing produced significant increases in MVC and TVR in affected quadriceps and biceps femoris muscles.

title: Does placebo response mediate runner's high?
abstract: It is proposed that runner's high is mediated by increased endorphin release as induced by placebo responses arising from subjective expectancies and setting.

screening.rationale: Paper proposed a theoretical hypothesis that runner's high is mediated by placebo responses/expectancy and setting, making placebo phenomena the explicit subject (theory piece).

classification.summary: Proposed that runner's high is mediated by endorphin release produced via placebo responses arising from expectancies and setting.

title: Can pregnancy be a placebo effect?: Terminology, designs, and conclusions in the study of psychosocial and pharmacological treatments of behavior disorders.
journal: Journal of behavior therapy and experimental psychiatry
abstract: This paper discusses several salient issues in the clinical research enterprise which were stimulated by chapters on research methods and placebo phenomena in White, Tursky and Schwartz (1985), Placebo: Theory, Research, and Mechanisms. These issues include the commonalities of questions, domains and classes of variables, and research strategies needed for the discovery, accumulation and application of knowledge regarding effective clinical treatments. Problems of unwarranted uniformity assumptions and absolute design requirements as well as the failure to attend to the conceptual relevance, strength and integrity of procedures are noted with examples from the systematic desensitization literature. Meta-analyses and indexes of effect size are also examined with examples demonstrating the need for especially cautious interpretation of these procedures. A re-emphasis of the construct validity approach with better designed and executed individual studies is endorsed as the best means to improve progress.

screening.rationale: Paper is a conceptual/methodological discussion focused on placebo phenomena, trial design, and interpretation in psychosocial and pharmacological treatment research (placebo science), so it meets inclusion criterion 5.

classification.summary: Argued for greater construct validity and careful design in studies of psychosocial and pharmacological treatments, discussed placebo phenomena and methodological issues in desensitization and meta-analysis interpretation.

title: Early placebo response in anxious and depressed patients.
abstract: Specific subgroups of anxiety disorder patients (N = 130) and depression patients (N = 105), defined according to DSM-III criteria, were given 1 week of placebo treatment as part of ongoing clinical drug trials. Placebo responses and dropout rates were assessed at the end of the placebo trial period. The results indicate a comparable dropout rate between depression and anxiety disorder groups due to positive placebo response, negative placebo response, and "nonsymptomatic" reasons. In addition, male anxiety disorder patients dropped out at a significantly higher rate than male depression patients.

screening.rationale: Placebo response during a 1-week placebo lead-in was the paper's analytic focus (assessed placebo responses and dropout rates), meeting the criterion for studying placebo responses.

classification.summary: Reported placebo responses and dropout rates after a 1-week placebo lead-in in patients with DSM-III anxiety disorders (N=130) and depression (N=105).
classification.key_finding: Found comparable placebo response and dropout rates across anxiety and depression groups, with male anxiety patients showing higher dropout than male depression patients.

title: Social and behavioral consequences of alcohol consumption and expectancy: a meta-analysis.

screening.rationale: Title identifies a meta-analysis explicitly about alcohol expectancy effects (placebo/expectancy is the paper's focus) meeting inclusion rule for meta-analyses of placebo/expectation phenomena.

classification.summary: Meta-analyzed studies of alcohol consumption and expectancy to assess how beliefs about alcohol influenced social and behavioral outcomes.

title: Placebo problems in psychotherapy research. Social-psychological alternatives to chemotherapy concepts.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses 'placebo problems in psychotherapy research' and proposes alternatives, indicating placebo is the main subject (theoretical/review focus).

classification.summary: Discussed conceptual and methodological problems of placebo controls in psychotherapy research and proposed social-psychological alternative frameworks to chemotherapy-based concepts.

title: Does placebo improve indexes of effort-induced myocardial ischemia? An objective study in 150 patients with chronic stable angina pectoris.
abstract: The effects of placebo were studied in 150 patients (135 men, 15 women) aged 42 to 75 years with stable exertional angina pectoris, using multistage graded exercise testing. Treadmill exercise, using on-line computer analysis of the electrocardiogram, was performed after a basal period, during which time the patients had no treatment for 2 weeks, and after 2 weeks of placebo therapy. Mean exercise time during no treatment was 6.0 +/- 0.2 minutes and during placebo was 6.1 +/- 0.2 minutes (difference not significant). Similarly, time to development of 1 mm of ST-segment depression of 4.0 +/- 0.2 minutes without treatment was 4.1 +/- 0.2 minutes after 2 weeks of placebo therapy (difference not significant). Placebo failed to show any effect on rest or maximal heart rate or on maximal ST-segment depression. It also failed to increase exercise tolerance or to improve other objective indexes of effort-induced myocardial ischemia in both single-and double-blind protocols in patients with stable exertional angina pectoris. Therefore, placebo control of antianginal drug trials that use exercise testing for evaluation of effect is unnecessary and can be omitted.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly tested placebo therapy versus a no-treatment baseline on objective ischemia measures in 150 patients, isolating the placebo effect.

classification.summary: Tested 2 weeks of oral placebo versus a no-treatment baseline in 150 patients with stable angina and found no improvement in exercise tolerance, ST-segment depression, or heart-rate indices.
classification.key_finding: Placebo did not significantly change exercise time, time to 1 mm ST-depression, maximal ST-depression, or heart rate.

title: Domperidone, metoclopramide, and placebo. All give symptomatic improvement in gastroesophageal reflux.
abstract: A double-blind crossover study was conducted of two gastric prokinetic drugs in 23 patients with gastroesophageal reflux. Patients were divided into two groups on the basis of a dual-isotope mixed-meal study of their gastric emptying (GE). Group I had normal GE and group II delayed GE. Nine gastrointestinal symptoms were assessed for frequency and severity before treatment. The trial had three 1-month treatment periods using metoclopramide 10 mg q.i.d., domperidone 20 mg q.i.d., or placebo on a random basis. Symptoms were reassessed at the end of each month. Taken as a whole, the group showed a significant symptomatic response in all three treatment periods (p less than 0.0001), but patients with delayed or normal GE did not differ significantly in their symptomatic response. Eleven patients complained of side effects with metoclopramide and three stopped therapy before the 1-month course was completed. Two patients described side effects with domperidone, including one woman with galactorrhea after 36 h of treatment. Three patients on placebo also complained of important side effects. We conclude that a significant placebo effect is present in the treatment of gastroesophageal reflux. No significant difference was demonstrated in symptomatic improvement between placebo, domperidone, and metoclopramide in this study.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind crossover trial reported symptomatic improvement in the placebo arm and concluded a significant placebo effect, so placebo response/effect was a substantive object of study.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind crossover RCT in 23 reflux patients and found significant symptomatic improvement during metoclopramide, domperidone, and placebo periods, with no differences between treatments.
classification.key_finding: No significant difference in symptom improvement between placebo, domperidone, and metoclopramide; substantial placebo response observed.

title: Placebo-like effects of education about rational-emotive therapy.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title implies placebo-like effects of education about REBT but available information is insufficient to confirm that placebo/nocebo phenomena were the study's explicit focus or that an experimental contrast was used.

classification.summary: Insufficient information (no abstract) to determine whether the study experimentally tested placebo/nocebo effects; title suggested education about rational-emotive therapy produced placebo-like effects.

title: Expectancy effects on relaxation instructions: physiological and self-report indices.
abstract: Two sessions of relaxation instructions were administered under high and low expectancy conditions. Fifty-four college students scoring high on a self-report measure of anxiety served as subjects. Live and taped abbreviated progressive muscle relaxation instructions and a self-relaxation condition were equally effective in reducing within-session self-report and physiological indices of anxiety. High expectancy instructions led to greater reductions in heart rate than did low expectancy instructions. Factors controlling anxiety reduction during relaxation therapies are discussed.

screening.rationale: Within-subject manipulation of expectancy (high vs low) was the experimental focus and produced differential physiological and self-report anxiety reductions, meeting the placebo/context effect inclusion criteria.

classification.summary: Compared high versus low expectancy relaxation instructions in 54 anxious college students and found greater heart-rate reductions and similar self-reported anxiety decreases across conditions, with high expectancy producing larger physiological change.
classification.key_finding: High-expectancy instructions produced greater reductions in heart rate than low-expectancy instructions; both reduced self-reported anxiety.

title: Older age treatment expectations.
abstract: The relationship between age and treatment expectation (TE) has been virtually ignored. This study assessed the TE and posthospital adjustment of 5,347 psychiatric patients, 4,361 younger (less than 55) and 986 older (greater than 55). Patients were evaluated on admission with self- and other rating adjustment scales and again at 3-months postdischarge. One factor in the self-rating scale included TE. Outcome measures involved posthospital adjustment (self- and other rated), both corrected and noncorrected for initial adjustment levels. Results show that TE rises with age. There is also some indication that higher TE leads to better adjustment. Older age and higher TE in combination, however, do not translate into better community adjustment. Also, differences between younger and older patients in TE are most pronounced in psychotics and in older patients not fully or currently employed.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly measured treatment expectations and tested their association with clinical outcomes, addressing expectation effects relevant to placebo science.

classification.summary: Assessed treatment expectations in 5,347 psychiatric inpatients and found expectations rose with age and were sometimes associated with better 3-month posthospital adjustment, though older age plus high expectation did not improve community adjustment.
classification.key_finding: Treatment expectation increased with age and was modestly associated with better posthospital adjustment, but this did not hold for older patients' community adjustment.

title: Method of administration determines the effect of naloxone on pain.
abstract: The opiate antagonist, naloxone, produces dose-dependent biphasic changes in clinical pain. The mechanism of the analgesia produced by low dose naloxone is unknown. To study the analgesic effect of naloxone, we have used a programmable infusion pump, which eliminates placebo-induced endorphin-mediated analgesia, to administer different doses of naloxone. We report that use of machine infusion of naloxone exclusively produces analgesia. The implications of this finding to the mechanism of naloxone-induced analgesia are discussed.

screening.rationale: Study used method-of-administration (machine vs. contextual administration) to probe naloxone analgesia, an open/hidden style manipulation of treatment context relevant to placebo mechanisms.

classification.summary: Compared methods of naloxone administration and found machine (hidden) infusion produced analgesia, implicating method/context and endogenous opioid mechanisms in analgesic effects.
classification.key_finding: Machine-administered naloxone produced analgesia whereas contextually administered drug did not, suggesting administration method modulates opioid-related placebo/analgesic effects.

title: A trial of amitriptyline and fluphenazine in the treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy.
abstract: We conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study of the effectiveness of amitriptyline and fluphenazine in alleviating the pain of diabetic peripheral neuropathy in six diabetic patients. Pain was evaluated by the patients with a graphic rating scale. A placebo response was found, but no additional effect of amitriptyline and fluphenazine was seen. Although the statistical power of this study was low, these data, when combined with a reevaluation of previous trials of amitriptyline and fluphenazine in the treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy, indicate that there is no justification for the use of these agents in the treatment of painful neuropathy outside of large, controlled clinical trials. Depression as a possible cause of this condition should not go unnoted or untreated.

screening.rationale: Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial that reported a measurable placebo response and examined placebo arm outcomes.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in six diabetic patients and found a placebo response on patient-reported pain but no additional benefit of amitriptyline or fluphenazine.
classification.key_finding: Found a significant placebo-related reduction in self-reported neuropathic pain but no drug-specific analgesic effect in this small sample.

title: Anti-inflammatory effects of ultrasound therapy: evidence for a major placebo effect.
abstract: The value of therapeutic ultrasound (US) for reducing inflammation was tested in a double-blind controlled study in 150 patients following surgical removal of impacted lower third molars. Facial swelling, trismus, pain and serum C-reactive protein (CRP) were significantly reduced in the US-treated groups and in a placebo group ('mock' US) compared with an untreated control group. The majority of the anti-inflammatory activity was attributable to the placebo effect, and the highest intensity of US (1.5 W.cm-2) was consistently less beneficial than the lower intensities (0.1 and 0.5 W.cm-2) and the mock US.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial explicitly contrasted mock (placebo) ultrasound against untreated control and concluded most anti-inflammatory benefit was attributable to the placebo (mock) intervention, making placebo effect a primary focus.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial in 150 patients after impacted third-molar extraction found ultrasound and mock (sham) ultrasound reduced pain, swelling, trismus and CRP versus no treatment, with most anti-inflammatory benefit attributable to the placebo (mock) intervention.
classification.key_finding: Mock (placebo) ultrasound produced reductions in clinical signs and CRP similar to or greater than higher-intensity ultrasound, indicating the majority of the effect was placebo-driven.

title: Counselor and client personality as determinants of counselor expectancy effects.
journal: Journal of personality and social psychology
abstract: Seventy-eight students enrolled in summer-session college courses were randomly assigned to serve either as counselors or as clients for a 20-min, role-played peer counseling session. All of the subjects completed a battery of standardized personality measures. Each counselor interacted with two clients. Prior to the sessions, the counselor was led to believe that one of the clients was especially introverted and that the other client was especially extraverted. Dependent measures were based on clients' change scores on a mood adjective rating scale administered before and after the peer counseling sessions. Analyses showed that counselors who were more successful at biasing their clients in the direction of their expectancies (a) scored higher on measures of Dogmatism, Nurturance, and Social Recognition, (b) scored lower on Impulsivity, and (c) were more likely to be women. Clients who were more susceptible to counselor bias scored higher on the Self-Monitoring Scale, the Self-Monitoring Other-Directedness subscale, and Social Recognition. These results are discussed in light of previous research and their implications for research on interpersonal expectancy effects.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of counselor expectancies produced changes in clients' mood ratings, making interpersonal expectancy effects the paper's primary focus (an experimentally isolated context/expectation effect).

classification.summary: Randomized role-play counseling manipulated counselors' beliefs about client personality and found clients' mood ratings shifted in the direction of counselors' expectancies.
classification.key_finding: Counselors successfully biased clients' pre-post mood change; counselor personality and gender and client self-monitoring predicted susceptibility.

title: Placebo controls in psychotherapy research: a sine qua non or a placebo for research problems?
journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper's main subject is placebo controls in psychotherapy research (a methodological/theoretical discussion), meeting inclusion for placebo science/theory.

classification.summary: Discussed the role, challenges, and utility of placebo controls in psychotherapy research and questioned their value for resolving methodological problems.

title: The placebo concept in medicine and psychiatry.
abstract: The standard technical vocabulary used to define placebo therapies and experimental placebo controls in medicine and psychiatry is both confusing and obscure. To achieve conceptual clarity in the theory of placebogenic phenomena, this paper offers a rigorous articulation of the placebo notion, a lucid new terminology that obviates the defects intrinsic to the traditional locutions employed in the placebo literature, and a substantial revamping of A. K. Shapiro's influential prior definition of 'placebo'. This paper supersedes an earlier version (Grünbaum, 1981).

screening.rationale: Paper's explicit aim is conceptual clarification of placebo phenomena and terminology, making placebo the main subject (theory/commentary).

classification.summary: Proposes a rigorous articulation and new terminology for placebo phenomena in medicine and psychiatry, revising prior definitions to improve conceptual clarity.

title: Placebo-controlled, blind study of dietary manipulation therapy in rheumatoid arthritis.
abstract: In a blind, placebo-controlled study of dietary manipulation therapy in outpatients with rheumatoid arthritis there was significant objective improvement during periods of dietary therapy compared with periods of placebo treatment, particularly among "good responders". Possible explanations for improvement include reduced food intolerance, reduced gastrointestinal permeability, and benefit from weight loss and from altered intake of substrates for prostaglandin production. A proportion of the improvement was due to a placebo response, but this was not sufficient to explain the whole improvement.

screening.rationale: Randomized, blind, placebo-controlled trial that explicitly reported and analyzed the proportion of improvement attributable to a placebo response in rheumatoid arthritis.

classification.summary: Randomized, blind, placebo-controlled trial of dietary manipulation in outpatients with rheumatoid arthritis that found significant objective improvement with diet and noted that a proportion of improvement was due to a placebo response.
classification.key_finding: Found significant objective improvement with dietary therapy versus placebo, with some improvement attributable to a placebo response.

title: Ultradian chronomodulation by melatonin of a Placebo effect upon human killer cell activity.
abstract: The effect of melatonin injection evaluated earlier with respect to placebo-treated controls is reevaluated, also with reference to spontaneous changes in natural killer cell activity. This effect consists, first, of stimulation of natural killer cell activity over and above any changes brought about by placebo (saline). After 6 h, the melatonin effect appears to be an inhibition as compared to values from placebo-treated subjects, or no effect as compared to values from untreated subjects. In this case, amplification and attenuation of the placebo effect by melatonin are found within the relatively short span of 1/4 of a day, rather than within a day or a week. An ultradian 'feed-sideward' by melatonin may be aligned with the corresponding previously reported circadian and infradian chronomodulation.

screening.rationale: Study explicitly analyzed and reported amplification/attenuation of a placebo (saline) effect on natural killer cell activity and compared placebo-treated versus untreated controls, so placebo phenomena were a focus.

classification.summary: Reanalyzed melatonin injection effects relative to saline placebo and untreated controls and found melatonin could amplify or attenuate the placebo-associated changes in natural killer cell activity over ultradian timescales.
classification.key_finding: Reported that melatonin produced initial stimulation above placebo-induced NK activity, then relative inhibition or no effect after 6 h, indicating ultradian modulation of the placebo effect.

title: The placebo control in clinical trials (a view from the FDA).
mesh: United States Food and Drug Administration

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper addresses the role of the placebo control in clinical trials (methodology/ policy), matching 'placebo_science_other' inclusion as placebo-focused science/methodology despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Discussed the FDA perspective on use and issues of placebo controls in clinical trials.

title: Scientific and ethical considerations in the use of placebo controls in clinical trials in psychopharmacology.

screening.rationale: Paper is a review/discussion of scientific and ethical use of placebo controls in psychopharmacology, so placebo is the main subject (placebo science/ethics).

classification.summary: Discussed scientific and ethical issues in using placebo controls in psychopharmacology clinical trials, focusing on research design and consent considerations.

title: Use of placebo in clinical trials.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title implies methodological discussion of placebo use but insufficient information to confirm that placebo effects/responses are the paper's explicit focus.

classification.summary: Discusses the use of placebos in clinical trials and related methodological issues (abstract not available).

title: Effects of therapeutic touch on tension headache pain.
abstract: Therapeutic touch (TT) is a modern derivative of the laying on of hands that involves touching with the intent to help or heal. This study investigated the effects of TT on tension headache pain in comparison with a placebo simulation of TT. Sixty volunteer subjects with tension headaches were randomly divided into treatment and placebo groups. The McGill-Melzack Pain Questionnaire was used to measure headache pain levels before each intervention, immediately afterward, and 4 hours later. A Wilcoxon signed rank test for differences indicated that 90% of the subjects exposed to TT experienced a sustained reduction in headache pain, p less than .0001. An average 70% pain reduction was sustained over the 4 hours following TT, which was twice the average pain reduction following the placebo touch. Using a Wilcoxon rank sum test, this was statistically significant, p less than .01. Study results indicated that TT may have potential beyond a placebo effect in the treatment of tension headache pain.

screening.rationale: Randomized sham-controlled trial that compared therapeutic touch with a placebo simulation and reported placebo-arm change and between-group differences, so the placebo/sham response is an object of analysis.

classification.summary: Found that therapeutic touch produced significantly greater reductions in tension headache pain than a placebo simulation, with a sustained 70% average reduction over 4 hours versus about half that in the placebo group (p < .01).
classification.key_finding: Therapeutic touch yielded a sustained 70% average pain reduction over 4 hours, approximately twice the reduction after placebo touch (p < .01); 90% of TT subjects showed sustained reduction (p < .0001 within-group).

title: NSAID ionisation in the management of soft-tissue rheumatism: role played by the drug, electrical stimulation and suggestion.
abstract: Four treatments for soft-tissue rheumatism--sham ionisation, placebo ionisation, and pharmacological ionisation with pirprofen (two-dose levels)--were assessed in a randomized double-blind, between-patient controlled trial in 73 outpatients affected by scapulo-humeral periarthritis or elbow epicondylitis. Treatment lasted two weeks (5 sessions a week). Progress was measured by patient's assessment on pain at rest and on movement and by physician's assessment on functional impairment. At two weeks each treatment was associated with a significant degree of improvement; however, pharmacological ionisation produced a significantly higher improvement in symptoms. No differences were detected between sham ionisation and placebo ionisation. These results suggest that the ionisation procedure displays per se a moderate therapeutic effect which seems to be due more to a simple placebo effect than to the biological effect of electricity.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial explicitly examined improvement in sham/placebo ionisation arms and discussed a placebo/suggestion-related effect as a major finding (placebo response investigated).

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial in 73 patients with periarthritis or epicondylitis found all arms improved over two weeks, with pharmacological ionisation producing greater symptom improvement while sham and placebo ionisation showed similar moderate benefit suggesting a placebo/suggestion effect.
classification.key_finding: All groups improved; drug ionisation yielded significantly greater improvement than sham/placebo, while sham and placebo ionisation did not differ, implying the ionisation procedure produced a moderate placebo response.

title: The therapeutic effect of clonidine in attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity: a comparison with placebo and methylphenidate.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial with placebo arm but no abstract/full text provided to determine whether placebo/nocebo effects or responses were analyzed.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial from 1986 compared clonidine, methylphenidate, and placebo in children with ADHD; abstract/full text not available to assess placebo-specific analyses.

title: Ethical questions raised by a proposed randomized, double-blind study involving placebo, standard drug therapy, and experimental antipsychotic drug therapy for patients with schizophrenia.

screening.rationale: Paper focused on ethical questions about using placebo in a proposed antipsychotic RCT, so it addresses placebo science (ethics) as the primary subject.

classification.summary: Discussed ethical issues raised by a proposed randomized, double-blind antipsychotic trial including a placebo arm for patients with schizophrenia.

title: Treatment of tinnitus by external electrical stimulation.
abstract: Transcutaneous electrical stimulation was used in 5 consecutive patients suffering from troublesome tinnitus. The study included three parts. Part one constituted an open trial using the stimulation equipment. During this part, 2 patients reported a reduced subjective tinnitus loudness. These 2 patients proceeded to part two where the effect from the stimulation equipment was compared with the effect from a placebo apparatus in an experimental double-blind trial.
